query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an ultra‐thin, conformal alumina coating via atomic layer deposition (ALD) on a refractory HEA will significantly improve its high‐temperature oxygen resistance by creating a pre‐formed, self-healing Al2O3 barrier that limits oxygen ingress.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high‐entropy alloy in its untreated state that forms a nonprotective, fast-growing oxide at extreme temperatures.
generation.intervention: Deposition of an ultra‐thin (10–50 nm) alumina coating via atomic layer deposition (ALD).
generation.conditions: Exposure at 1000–1200°C in an oxygen-rich atmosphere for durations exceeding 100 hours, consistent with extreme service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A nanoscale interfacial alumina (Al2O3) layer that adheres to the alloy surface and acts as an oxygen diffusion barrier without altering the bulk alloy composition.
generation.mechanism: The pre-deposited alumina layer serves as a protective, self-healing barrier that retards oxygen diffusion into the substrate. This limits further oxidation and preserves the material’s structural integrity, decoupling oxidation resistance from bulk mechanical features.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ALD-coated alloy will exhibit a markedly lower oxidation rate—evidenced by reduced mass gain and thinner, more adherent oxide scales—compared to the untreated alloy under identical high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory HEA, which under high-temperature, oxygen-rich conditions develops a rapidly growing and nonprotective oxide scale that compromises structural performance.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected as long as the coating remains intact under thermal stresses; potential challenges include coating degradation due to mechanical damage or thermal mismatch at temperatures significantly above 1200°C or under fluctuating load conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While the protective mechanism is well established in related high-temperature alloys, uncertainties remain regarding the long-term adhesion and thermal stability of such a thin ALD-deposited alumina layer on complex HEA surfaces over extended exposure beyond 100 hours and under mechanical load.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical refractory HEA samples. Apply a 10–50 nm ALD alumina coating on one set while leaving the other uncoated. Subject both sets to an oxygen-rich atmosphere at 1100°C for 100+ hours. Regularly measure mass gain and perform post-exposure microstructural analyses (SEM, XRD, and adhesion testing) of the oxide scales.
measurements: Mass gain per unit area over time
Oxide layer thickness and continuity (via cross-sectional SEM)
Phase identification of the oxide scale (via XRD)
Adhesion quality of the oxide layer (e.g., scratch testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ALD-coated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation rate (i.e., lower mass gain and improved oxide scale stability) compared to uncoated samples under identical high-temperature conditions, or if the alumina coating fails to remain adherent and protective, then the hypothesis is falsified.

4.1. Phase Stability at High Temperature

HEAs produced on casting when exposed to long-term annealing cause decomposition into the traditional multi-phase microstructure. The alloys decomposition on annealing at a higher temperature creates doubt about its applicability for high-temperature application (over 800 °C). Thermodynamic calculations were performed to understand whether the solid solution established when cast is a thermodynamically stable phase at potential use temperatures. Phase equilibria of CrMnFeCoNi alloy are visualized in Figure 9 as a one-dimensional step diagram of phase fractions and a function of temperature. From Figure 9 the critical features of phase equilibria are readily discernible, such as the thickness of the HEA’s single-phase FCC region (solvus to the solidus) at high temperature from solidus at 1320 °C down to about 750 °C. Also, it shows the lower temperature decomposition products stated in some works. At a lower temperature, phase equilibria show the formation of the sigma phase and BCC phase.

Since the distribution of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 were not continuous, neither Al 2 O 3 nor Cr 2 O 3 could provide effective barrier against oxidation in this study. At 1000 °C, the oxidation kinetic curve of NV1 alloy followed exponential dependence. Such dependence is usually observed in either during the initial stage of oxidation or oxidation at relatively lower temperatures [20] . frame.system: Refractory high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) designed for structural use at extreme temperatures; the starting state is an untreated alloy that inadequately resists oxygen-induced degradation.
frame.goal: Enhance high-temperature oxygen resistance by forming a stable, adherent protective oxide layer during service.
frame.limitation: The current alloy lacks a self-healing or slowly growing oxide scale at extreme temperatures, leading to rapid oxidation and degradation.
constraints: only a single intervention is allowed
intervention should be applicable without a wholesale change in composition (i.e., no complete alloy redesign)
frame.regime: Exposure at high temperatures (~1000–1200°C) in an oxygen-rich atmosphere for extended durations (e.g., 100+ hours) typical of extreme service conditions
prior_attempts: Bulk alloying with oxidation‐resistant elements (e.g., Cr, Al, Si) has been attempted, but these approaches often degraded mechanical properties or did not yield a sufficiently protective oxide scale.

decision.trend: Early efforts to improve oxygen resistance in refractory high‐entropy alloys have focused on altering the bulk composition through the addition of oxidation‐resistant elements such as Cr, Al, or Si. For example, one study varied the Cr content via laser cladding to refine the microstructure and form oxide‐bearing phases, while another detailed the oxidation mechanisms in a five-element HEA to understand why non‐protective mixed oxides (rather than continuous, self‐healing scales) form. These bulk alloying strategies have shown some reduction in oxidation rates but have not achieved a truly stable, adherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer, and in many cases, the mechanical properties are compromised.
decision.unsolved: A protective, self-healing oxide scale that effectively slows oxygen ingress at extreme temperatures (~1000–1200°C) without sacrificing the bulk structural integrity remains elusive. The challenge is to decouple oxidation resistance from the mechanical performance, something that bulk composition modifications have not fully solved.
decision.lever: Apply an ultra-thin, conformal alumina coating via atomic layer deposition (ALD)
decision.why: Building on the insight that bulk alloying has been unable to form a self-healing and slow-growing protective oxide without degrading mechanical properties, the next logical step is to engineer the alloy’s surface. A nanoscale ALD alumina layer (10–50 nm) would pre-form a protective Al2O3 film that activates under high-temperature, oxygen-rich conditions (1000–1200°C, 100+ hours exposure) to inhibit further oxidation, as established in conventional high-temperature alloys. This approach leverages surface modification to achieve the desired oxidation resistance while leaving the bulk alloy composition—and thus its mechanical integrity—unchanged.
